title: Operating Systems & System Design
description: Modern Interview Revision Cheat Sheet covering OS fundamentals, processes, threads, concurrency, deadlock, virtual memory, and core system design concepts.

sections.title: PART 1: OPERATING SYSTEMS
sections.description: OS fundamentals, process management, concurrency, synchronization, deadlocks, and memory management.

topics.title: 1. Fundamentals of Operating Systems (OS)
topics.explanation:
🖥️ What is an Operating System?
An Operating System (OS) is the main system software that acts as a bridge between computer hardware and applications[cite: 4].
It manages hardware resources and provides services that allow applications to run without directly controlling hardware[cite: 4].

The OS Manages:
CPU
RAM / Memory
Storage
Input/Output devices
Processes
Files
Network resources[cite: 4]

Basic Architecture:
Applications
     ↓
Operating System
     ↓
Hardware[cite: 4]

Without an OS, application developers would need to write complex hardware-specific code to perform basic operations[cite: 4].

Examples of Operating Systems:
Windows
Linux
macOS
Android
iOS[cite: 4]

Main Responsibilities of an OS:
1️⃣ Process Management: Creates processes, Schedules processes, Allocates CPU time, Terminates processes[cite: 4]
2️⃣ Memory Management: Allocates memory, Frees unused memory, Manages virtual memory, Protects process memory[cite: 4]
3️⃣ File Management: Manages files, Directories, Storage permissions[cite: 4]
4️⃣ Device Management: Communicates with Keyboard, Mouse, Disk, Printer, Network devices[cite: 4]
topics.tldr: OS হলো Hardware আর Application-এর মাঝখানের manager, যা computer-এর সব resource manage করে[cite: 4]。

questions.question: Is an Operating System just software for running applications?
questions.answer: No. An OS also manages hardware resources, processes, memory, files, devices, and security[cite: 4].

traps.statement: An Operating System is just software for running applications.
traps.explanation: No. An OS also manages hardware resources, processes, memory, files, devices, and security[cite: 4].

topics.title: 2. Process vs Thread & 3. Process vs Thread — Comparison
topics.explanation:
🔵 Process
A Process is a program that is currently executing[cite: 4].
Each process normally has its own:
Memory space
Resources
Execution context[cite: 4]
Example: If you open Chrome, VS Code, Spotify, they usually run as separate processes[cite: 4].
Process Concept: Program → Execution Starts → Process[cite: 4]
Normally: Process A ✗ Cannot directly access Process B Memory[cite: 4]

🟢 Thread
A Thread is the smallest unit of execution inside a process[cite: 4].
A process can contain multiple threads[cite: 4].
Threads inside the same process typically share: Code, Heap memory, Global variables, Open resources[cite: 4].
However, each thread has its own: Stack, Registers, Program counter[cite: 4].
Example: A browser may use different threads for User interface, Rendering, Background tasks, Network operations[cite: 4].
topics.tldr: Process হলো চলমান পুরো program, আর Thread হলো সেই program-এর ভিতরের execution unit[cite: 4]। Process আলাদা memory ব্যবহার করে, Thread একই process-এর memory share করে[cite: 4]。

questions.question: Do threads share everything?
questions.answer: No. Threads typically share process resources such as code and heap, but each thread has its own stack, registers, and execution state[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Threads share everything within a process.
traps.explanation: No. Threads typically share process resources such as code and heap, but each thread has its own stack, registers, and execution state[cite: 4].

topics.title: 4. Process Lifecycle
topics.explanation:
A process moves through different states while executing[cite: 4].

Process States Flow:
New → Ready → Running → Waiting / Blocked → Ready → Running → Terminated[cite: 4]

🆕 New
The process is being created by the OS[cite: 4]. Program → Process Creation → New[cite: 4]

🟡 Ready
The process is ready to run but is waiting for CPU time[cite: 4]. Ready → Waiting for CPU[cite: 4]

🟢 Running
The CPU is currently executing the process[cite: 4]. CPU → Executing Process[cite: 4]

🔵 Waiting / Blocked
The process cannot continue until an event occurs[cite: 4].
Examples: File read, Database response, Network response, User input, Disk I/O[cite: 4]. Process → Waiting for I/O → Blocked[cite: 4]

🔴 Terminated
The process has finished normally, or been stopped because of an error[cite: 4]. The OS then releases its resources[cite: 4].
topics.tldr: Ready মানে CPU পাওয়ার অপেক্ষায়, আর Waiting/Blocked মানে কোনো event বা I/O-এর অপেক্ষায়[cite: 4]。

questions.question: What is the difference between Ready and Waiting?
questions.answer: A Ready process is waiting only for CPU time. A Waiting/Blocked process is waiting for an external event or resource, such as I/O completion[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Ready and Waiting are the same state.
traps.explanation: A Ready process is waiting only for CPU time. A Waiting/Blocked process is waiting for an external event or resource, such as I/O completion[cite: 4].

topics.title: 5. Context Switching
topics.explanation:
🔄 What is Context Switching?
Context Switching happens when the OS pauses one process or thread and switches the CPU to another[cite: 4].
The OS saves the current execution state and restores the state of another process or thread[cite: 4].

Context May Include:
CPU registers
Program counter
Stack information
Process/thread state[cite: 4]

Flow:
Process A Running → Save Context → Load Context → Process B Running[cite: 4]

Why is Context Switching Needed?
It enables: Multitasking, Fair CPU scheduling, Responsive systems, Concurrent execution[cite: 4].

Performance Cost:
Context switching has overhead[cite: 4].
CPU Time → Save State → Load State → Resume Another Task[cite: 4]
During switching, the CPU is not doing useful application work[cite: 4]. Frequent context switching can reduce performance[cite: 4].
topics.tldr: এক process/thread pause করে আরেকটাকে CPU দেওয়াই Context Switching[cite: 4]。

questions.question: Is context switching free?
questions.answer: No. It has performance overhead because the OS must save and restore execution state, and frequent switching can reduce efficiency[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Context switching has zero performance overhead.
traps.explanation: No. It has performance overhead because the OS must save and restore execution state, and frequent switching can reduce efficiency[cite: 4].

topics.title: 6. Multiprocessing vs Multithreading
topics.explanation:
🖥️ Multiprocessing
Multiprocessing uses multiple processes[cite: 4]. Each process has separate memory and stronger isolation[cite: 4].
Advantages: Better isolation, Can use multiple CPU cores, One process crash may not affect others[cite: 4].
Disadvantages: Higher memory usage, IPC can be more expensive[cite: 4].

🧵 Multithreading
Multithreading uses multiple threads inside one process[cite: 4].
Advantages: Lightweight, Fast communication, Shared memory[cite: 4].
Disadvantages: Race conditions, Synchronization complexity, A serious process failure can affect all threads[cite: 4].
topics.tldr: Multiprocessing = আলাদা আলাদা process, Multithreading = একই process-এর ভিতরে অনেক thread[cite: 4]。

questions.question: Does multithreading always mean true parallel execution?
questions.answer: No. Concurrency and parallelism are different. True parallel execution depends on factors such as CPU cores and how threads are scheduled[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Multithreading always means true parallel execution.
traps.explanation: No. Concurrency and parallelism are different. True parallel execution depends on factors such as CPU cores and how threads are scheduled[cite: 4].

topics.title: 7. Concurrency and Synchronization
topics.explanation:
When multiple threads access shared resources, problems can occur[cite: 4].
Example: Shared Balance = $100. Thread A → Withdraw $50, Thread B → Withdraw $50. Without proper synchronization: Race Condition ❌[cite: 4]

⚠️ Race Condition
A Race Condition happens when multiple threads access shared data concurrently and the final result depends on execution timing[cite: 4].
Example:
Counter = 0
Thread A → Reads 0
Thread B → Reads 0
Thread A → Writes 1
Thread B → Writes 1
Final Result = 1 ❌ (Expected = 2)[cite: 4]

🔒 Mutex
A Mutex is a synchronization mechanism that allows only one thread to access a critical section at a time[cite: 4].
Flow:
Thread A → Lock → Access Shared Data → Unlock
Thread B → Wait for Lock[cite: 4]
topics.tldr: একই shared data একসাথে অনেক thread change করলে race condition হতে পারে। Mutex দিয়ে একবারে একজনকে access দেওয়া হয়[cite: 4]。

questions.question: Does shared memory make multithreading easier?
questions.answer: Communication is faster, but shared memory introduces synchronization problems such as race conditions and deadlocks[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Shared memory makes multithreading completely straightforward and problem-free.
traps.explanation: Communication is faster, but shared memory introduces synchronization problems such as race conditions and deadlocks[cite: 4].

topics.title: 8. Deadlock, 9. The Four Coffman Conditions & 10. Deadlock Prevention
topics.explanation:
8. Deadlock
🔒 What is Deadlock?
A Deadlock happens when two or more processes or threads are permanently waiting for each other, so none of them can continue[cite: 4].
Simple Example: Process A holds Resource 1 and waits for Resource 2; Process B holds Resource 2 and waits for Resource 1. Result: Both Wait Forever ❌[cite: 4]

9. The Four Coffman Conditions
A deadlock can occur only when all four conditions exist at the same time[cite: 4]:
1️⃣ Mutual Exclusion: A resource can be used by only one process or thread at a time[cite: 4].
2️⃣ Hold and Wait: A process holds one resource while waiting for another[cite: 4].
3️⃣ No Preemption: The resource cannot simply be forcefully taken away; the process must release it[cite: 4].
4️⃣ Circular Wait: Processes form a circular dependency (e.g., A → B → C → A)[cite: 4].
Remember: M H N C[cite: 4]

10. How to Prevent Deadlock
Deadlock prevention means breaking at least one Coffman condition[cite: 4].
Common Approaches:
- Break Hold and Wait: Request all required resources at once[cite: 4].
- Break Circular Wait: Require resources to be requested in a fixed order (e.g., Always Lock Resource A Before Resource B)[cite: 4].
- Allow Preemption: In some situations, resources can be released or reassigned[cite: 4].
Deadlock Handling Strategies: 1. Prevention, 2. Avoidance, 3. Detection and Recovery, 4. Ignore It[cite: 4].
topics.tldr: চারটা condition একসাথে থাকলে deadlock হতে পারে[cite: 4]。

questions.question: Can deadlock occur if one Coffman condition is missing?
questions.answer: No. All four Coffman conditions must be present for a classic deadlock to occur[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Deadlock can still occur even if one of the Coffman conditions is broken.
traps.explanation: No. All four Coffman conditions must be present for a classic deadlock to occur[cite: 4].

topics.title: 11. Virtual Memory, 12. Paging, 13. Page Fault & 14. Thrashing
topics.explanation:
11. Virtual Memory
Virtual Memory allows each process to use a large virtual address space while the OS manages the mapping to physical memory and storage[cite: 4]. Allows running programs even when total memory exceeds available RAM[cite: 4].
Flow: Program → Virtual Memory → OS Memory Management → RAM + Disk Storage[cite: 4]

12. Paging
Paging divides memory into fixed-size blocks[cite: 4]:
- Pages: Fixed-size block of virtual memory[cite: 4].
- Frames: Fixed-size block of physical RAM[cite: 4].
The OS maps pages to frames to simplify allocation, support virtual memory, reduce external fragmentation, and allow non-contiguous allocation[cite: 4].

13. Page Fault
⚠️ What is a Page Fault?
A Page Fault occurs when a program tries to access a memory page that is not currently loaded into physical RAM[cite: 4].
Flow: Program Requests Page → Page Not in RAM → Page Fault → OS Locates Page → Load into RAM → Resume Program[cite: 4].
Important Point: Page Fault ≠ Program Error. It is a normal part of virtual memory management unless excessive[cite: 4].

14. Thrashing
🔥 What is Thrashing?
Thrashing happens when the system spends most of its time moving pages between RAM and storage instead of executing useful work[cite: 4].
Causes: Not enough RAM, too many running processes, excessive memory usage, poor memory management[cite: 4].
Solutions: Add more RAM, reduce running processes, improve memory usage, adjust system memory management[cite: 4].
topics.tldr: Virtual Memory-এর block হলো Page, আর RAM-এর block হলো Frame[cite: 4]। দরকারি page RAM-এ না থাকলে Page Fault হয়, OS সেটাকে load করে[cite: 4]। RAM কম হলে system বারবার RAM আর disk-এর মধ্যে data আনা-নেওয়া করে, তাই computer খুব slow হয়ে যায়[cite: 4]。

questions.question: Are pages and frames the same thing?
questions.answer: They are both fixed-size blocks, but a page belongs to virtual memory while a frame belongs to physical RAM[cite: 4].

questions.question: Does a page fault mean the application crashed?
questions.answer: No. A page fault is normally handled by the operating system. It becomes a serious performance issue only when page faults happen excessively[cite: 4].

questions.question: What is the difference between a page fault and thrashing?
questions.answer: A page fault is a single event where a required page is not in RAM. Thrashing is excessive paging that severely reduces system performance[cite: 4].

traps.statement: A page fault means the application crashed.
traps.explanation: No. A page fault is normally handled by the operating system. It becomes a serious performance issue only when page faults happen excessively[cite: 4].

topics.title: OS Rapid Revision Flashcards
topics.explanation: Rapid revision flashcards covering core operating system interview concepts[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: What is an Operating System?
flashcards.answer: An OS manages hardware resources and provides services that allow applications to run (Applications → Operating System → Hardware)[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: Process vs Thread?
flashcards.answer: Process = Independent Program Execution + Separate Memory. Thread = Execution Unit Inside Process + Shared Process Resources[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: What is Context Switching?
flashcards.answer: The OS saves the state of one process/thread and loads another so the CPU can switch execution[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: What are the four Coffman conditions?
flashcards.answer: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: What is a Page Fault?
flashcards.answer: A required memory page is not currently in RAM, so the OS loads it from storage[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: What is Thrashing?
flashcards.answer: Excessive paging between RAM and disk causes the system to spend more time managing memory than executing programs[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: Ready vs Waiting?
flashcards.answer: Ready = Waiting for CPU. Waiting / Blocked = Waiting for Event or I/O[cite: 4].

sections.title: PART 2: SYSTEM DESIGN FUNDAMENTALS
sections.description: Scalability, load balancing, architectural patterns, reliability, and high availability.

topics.title: 15. What is System Design?, 16. Scalability, 17. Vertical Scaling & 18. Horizontal Scaling
topics.explanation:
15. What is System Design?
System Design is the process of designing the architecture, components, interfaces, data flow, and infrastructure of a software system[cite: 4].
Focuses on building systems that are: Scalable, Reliable, Available, Maintainable, Performant[cite: 4].
Example: Users → Load Balancer → Application Servers → Database → Cache / Storage[cite: 4]

16. Scalability
Scalability is the ability of a system to handle increased workload without unacceptable performance degradation[cite: 4]. Approaches: Vertical Scaling and Horizontal Scaling[cite: 4].

17. Vertical Scaling — Scale Up
Vertical Scaling means making one server more powerful (upgrade CPU, RAM, Storage)[cite: 4].
Advantages: Simple architecture, easy to implement, less distributed-system complexity[cite: 4].
Disadvantages: Hardware limits, expensive, single point of failure, limited scaling capacity[cite: 4].

18. Horizontal Scaling — Scale Out
Horizontal Scaling means adding more servers and distributing workload between them (Users → Load Balancer → Server 1..4)[cite: 4].
Advantages: Handles larger workloads, better availability, better fault tolerance, can add servers gradually[cite: 4].
Disadvantages: More complex architecture, requires coordination, distributed data challenges, operational complexity[cite: 4].
topics.tldr: System Design হলো অনেক user এবং বড় traffic handle করার জন্য পুরো system-এর architecture plan করা[cite: 4]। একই server-কে আরও powerful করা = Vertical Scaling[cite: 4]। Server powerful করার বদলে নতুন নতুন server add করা = Horizontal Scaling[cite: 4]。

questions.question: Is horizontal scaling always better than vertical scaling?
questions.answer: No. Vertical scaling is often simpler and suitable for smaller systems. Horizontal scaling is useful when higher scale, availability, or fault tolerance is required[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Horizontal scaling is always superior to vertical scaling for all systems.
traps.explanation: No. Vertical scaling is often simpler and suitable for smaller systems. Horizontal scaling is useful when higher scale, availability, or fault tolerance is required[cite: 4].

topics.title: 20. Load Balancer
topics.explanation:
⚖️ What is a Load Balancer?
A Load Balancer sits between clients and backend servers and distributes incoming requests across available servers[cite: 4].
Architecture: Users → Load Balancer → Server 1, Server 2, Server 3[cite: 4]

Benefits:
⚡ Performance: Traffic is distributed (e.g. 1000 requests divided across 3 servers)[cite: 4].
🛡️ Reliability: If Server 2 fails, traffic is routed to Server 1 & 3[cite: 4].
📈 Scalability: New servers can be added during high traffic[cite: 4].

Common Load Balancing Strategies:
- Round Robin: Requests are distributed sequentially (Request 1 → Server A, Request 2 → Server B, etc.)[cite: 4].
- Least Connections: Send new requests to the server with fewer active connections[cite: 4].

questions.question: Does a Load Balancer automatically solve every scalability problem?
questions.answer: No. Backend services, databases, caching, and other infrastructure components may also become bottlenecks[cite: 4].

traps.statement: A Load Balancer automatically solves every scalability problem.
traps.explanation: No. Backend services, databases, caching, and other infrastructure components may also become bottlenecks[cite: 4].

topics.title: 21. Monolithic, 22. Microservices Architecture, 23. Comparison & 24. API Gateway
topics.explanation:
21. Monolithic Architecture
A Monolithic application contains major application features inside one deployable application (Auth, Products, Orders, Payments, Notifications)[cite: 4].
Advantages: Simple to build/deploy initially, easier for small teams, easier testing[cite: 4].
Disadvantages: Large codebase can become difficult to maintain, scaling individual features is difficult, tight coupling[cite: 4].

22. Microservices Architecture
Divides an application into smaller services focusing on specific business responsibilities[cite: 4]. Services communicate via HTTP APIs, gRPC, Message queues, Event streams[cite: 4].
Architecture: Users → API Gateway / Load Balancer → User Service, Product Service, Order Service, Payment Service[cite: 4].
Advantages: Independent development, independent scaling, fault isolation[cite: 4].
Disadvantages: Infrastructure complexity, network communication failures, distributed debugging, data consistency challenges[cite: 4].

24. API Gateway
Acts as an entry point for clients (Client → API Gateway → Specific Services)[cite: 4].
Responsibilities include: Request routing, Authentication, Rate limiting, Logging, Response aggregation[cite: 4].
topics.tldr: সব feature এক application-এর ভিতরে থাকলে সেটাই Monolith[cite: 4]। বড় application-কে ছোট ছোট independent service-এ ভাগ করলে সেটা Microservices[cite: 4]。

questions.question: Is Monolithic architecture always bad for large systems?
questions.answer: No. A well-designed monolith can scale significantly and is often simpler than microservices. Architecture should match the system's needs[cite: 4].

questions.question: Should every application use Microservices?
questions.answer: No. Microservices add significant operational complexity. For many small or medium applications, a modular monolith may be a better starting point[cite: 4].

questions.question: Is an API Gateway required for every microservices architecture?
questions.answer: No. It is a common pattern, but the architecture depends on system requirements[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Microservices is automatically a better architecture for every application.
traps.explanation: No. Microservices add significant operational complexity. For many small or medium applications, a modular monolith may be a better starting point[cite: 4].

topics.title: 25-28. Reliability, Availability, SPOF & Large-Scale Flow
topics.explanation:
25. Reliability vs Availability
Reliability: A system consistently performs correctly over time without unexpected failures[cite: 4].
Availability: Measures whether a system is accessible and operational when needed (e.g. 99.9% uptime)[cite: 4].
Difference: A system may be available but return incorrect results, so availability does not automatically mean reliability[cite: 4].

26. High Availability
Designing a system to minimize downtime using multiple servers, load balancers, failover, replication, health checks, backups[cite: 4].

27. Single Point of Failure (SPOF)
A component whose failure can cause the entire system to fail[cite: 4]. Reduced using redundant servers, load balancers, replication, and failover[cite: 4].

28. Basic Large-Scale System Design Flow
Simplified Architecture: Users → DNS → Load Balancer → Application Servers → Cache → Database → Storage[cite: 4]
Large Systems: Users → CDN → Load Balancer → API Gateway → Microservices → Cache → Databases → Message Queue → Background Workers[cite: 4]
topics.tldr: Available মানে system চালু আছে, Reliable মানে system ঠিকমতো consistently কাজ করছে[cite: 4]。

questions.question: Does adding multiple application servers remove all single points of failure?
questions.answer: No. Other components such as the load balancer, database, or network infrastructure may still be single points of failure unless they are also designed for redundancy[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Adding multiple application servers removes all single points of failure.
traps.explanation: No. Other components such as the load balancer, database, or network infrastructure may still be single points of failure unless they are also designed for redundancy[cite: 4].

topics.title: System Design Flashcards, Cheatsheet & Memory Map
topics.explanation:
🚀 INTERVIEW ONE-MINUTE SUMMARY & FINAL CHEAT SHEET
OS: Manages hardware and application resources[cite: 4]
Process: Independent running program[cite: 4]
Thread: Execution unit inside a process[cite: 4]
Ready: Waiting for CPU[cite: 4]
Blocked: Waiting for I/O/event[cite: 4]
Context Switch: Switch CPU between tasks[cite: 4]
Race Condition: Concurrent access causes unpredictable result[cite: 4]
Mutex: Controls critical section access[cite: 4]
Deadlock: Tasks wait indefinitely for each other[cite: 4]
Coffman Conditions: 4 required deadlock conditions (Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait)[cite: 4]
Virtual Memory: OS-managed virtual address space[cite: 4]
Page: Virtual memory block[cite: 4]
Frame: Physical RAM block[cite: 4]
Page Fault: Required page not in RAM[cite: 4]
Thrashing: Excessive paging[cite: 4]
Vertical Scaling: Scale Up[cite: 4]
Horizontal Scaling: Scale Out[cite: 4]
Load Balancer: Distributes traffic[cite: 4]
Monolith: One application[cite: 4]
Microservices: Multiple independent services[cite: 4]
SPOF: One failure can break the system[cite: 4]
High Availability: Minimize downtime[cite: 4]

🧠 GOLDEN INTERVIEW RULES
Process ≠ Thread[cite: 4]
Ready ≠ Waiting[cite: 4]
Page Fault ≠ Program Crash[cite: 4]
Concurrency ≠ Always Parallelism[cite: 4]
Horizontal Scaling ≠ Automatically Scalable Database[cite: 4]
Microservices ≠ Automatically Better Architecture[cite: 4]
Load Balancer ≠ Solution to Every Bottleneck[cite: 4]
topics.tldr: OS-এর মূল কাজ হলো CPU, Memory এবং Process manage করা। আর System Design-এর মূল লক্ষ্য হলো বেশি user এবং traffic handle করার জন্য scalable, reliable এবং available architecture তৈরি করা[cite: 4]。

flashcards.question: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling?
flashcards.answer: Vertical = More Powerful Server. Horizontal = More Servers[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: What does a Load Balancer do?
flashcards.answer: It distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: What is a Monolith?
flashcards.answer: A single application containing multiple features and responsibilities[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: What are Microservices?
flashcards.answer: Small services that independently handle specific business responsibilities and communicate through APIs or other mechanisms[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: What is a Single Point of Failure?
flashcards.answer: A component whose failure can cause the entire system or service to become unavailable[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: Why use Horizontal Scaling?
flashcards.answer: To handle increased traffic by adding more servers and improving availability and fault tolerance[cite: 4].

flashcards.question: Is Microservices always better than a Monolith?
flashcards.answer: No. Microservices provide flexibility but introduce significant complexity. A monolith is often better for simpler applications or early development[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Process is the same as Thread.
traps.explanation: Process ≠ Thread. A process is an independent program with its own memory space, while a thread is an execution unit inside a process sharing process resources[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Ready state is the same as Waiting state.
traps.explanation: Ready ≠ Waiting. Ready waits for CPU time, while Waiting waits for external events or I/O[cite: 4].

traps.statement: Page Fault equals a program crash.
traps.explanation: Page Fault ≠ Program Crash. A page fault is a routine virtual memory handling event[cite: 4].
Concurrency ≠ Always Parallelism. True parallel execution requires multiple CPU cores and appropriate scheduling[cite: 4].
